item.title: Migros gives more independence to the online and changes the top management
item.description: The Migros group reorganizes the structures creating the independent Online Retail sector and appoints Florian Teuteberg as new president.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Migros modifies structures and changes managers - The independent Online Retail sector is born - Matthias Wunderlin leaves office on the Board - Florian Teuteberg new president of Migros Online
## Key facts - Company: Migros Online - New sector: Online Retail - Replaces: Non Food - Outgoing Chairman of the Board: Matthias Wunderlin - New Chairman of the Board: Florian Teuteberg - CEO Digitec Galaxus: Florian Teuteberg
The retail giant Migros has announced a new reorganisation of its internal structures, introducing important changes at managerial and corporate level. At the center of the reorganization is the company Migros Online, which in the future will operate even more autonomously than in the past. As communicated by the Migros Federation of Cooperatives, the company will be managed as an independent entity within a completely new sector of activity called Online Retail. This new sector effectively replaces the current Non-Food sector within the Swiss group's organisation. The other three strategic branches that make up the group, namely Food Retail, Health and Financial Services, will not undergo any structural changes and will continue to operate according to the current approach. The decision reflects the management's willingness to adapt operating models to the changing conditions of the digital market and the consumption habits of Swiss customers.
### The details The profound structural reorganization announced by the large retail group inevitably involves important changes at the top of the company and within the supervisory bodies. Following this reshuffle, Matthias Wunderlin, who has so far served as chairman of the board of directors of Migros Online, will leave his post along with two other members of the supervisory body. The departure of these executives paves the way for a new phase of governance for the company active in food electronic commerce. The chairmanship of the board of directors is in fact entrusted to Florian Teuteberg, who already holds the role of CEO and co-founder of Digitec Galaxus and who was already part of the board of directors of Migros Online since 2018. This appointment represents a clear signal of the integration of digital skills within the Swiss group's decision-making leadership.
### The new members of the board of directors
Alongside the appointment of the new president, Migros Online's supervisory body is enriched with two new faces that bring a wealth of leading technical and commercial skills to the company. Oliver Herren, who is co-founder of Digitec Galaxus and responsible for innovation, and Hendrik Blenken Blijdenstein, currently responsible for the commercial sector, officially join the board.

The transition towards a more autonomous organizational model in the e-commerce sector represents a key step for the Swiss group, which aims to consolidate its presence on the national market through targeted management. ### Scenarios and Prospects for Consumers
For Swiss consumers who regularly use digital platforms for groceries and technology purchases, the changes at the top and the new corporate structure promise an increasingly specialized offering. item.title: The Federal Council presents the objectives for 2027
item.description: President Guy Parmelin outlined in Bern the strategic priorities for 2027, the fourth year of the 2023-2027 federal legislature.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - President Guy Parmelin presented the Federal Council's objectives for 2027 - Priorities for the fourth year of the 2023-2027 legislative term presented in Bern - Targeted strategies for economy, transport, security, and agriculture
## Key facts Press release date -> September 14, 2026 Presented by -> President of the Confederation Guy Parmelin Presentation venue -> Council of States, Bern Reference period -> Year 2027 Legislative program -> 2023-2027
President of the Confederation Guy Parmelin officially presented the objectives set by the Federal Council for the year 2027 to the Council of States. The speech took place in Bern and outlined the strategic priorities for the fourth and final year of the legislative program covering the 2023-2027 four-year term. The Swiss executive plans its activities annually through concrete and measurable goals, the results of which are subsequently verified and reported in the corresponding official management report.
### Federal strategic planning The definition of these objectives constitutes a central element of the Confederation's institutional planning. It allows federal authorities to coordinate legislative and administrative activities in a transparent manner. For 2027, the Government has structured a series of targeted interventions ranging from economic promotion to social reforms, outlining a programmatic framework extending to various federal departments and areas of Swiss public life. Annual programming serves to give concrete implementation to the four general political guidelines established at the beginning of the current legislative term, orienting state action toward objectives of sustainability, cohesion, security, and environmental protection.
### Underlying political guidelines During the 2023-2027 legislative term, the Federal Council's action is based on four fundamental strategic directions. The first direction establishes that Switzerland must ensure its prosperity in a sustainable manner, fully seizing the opportunities offered by digital technology. The second direction promotes national and intergenerational cohesion within the country. The third direction guarantees security, actively promotes peace, and ensures coherent and reliable action at the international level. Finally, the fourth direction is dedicated to climate protection and the safeguarding of the nation's natural resources. These four pillars are accompanied by twenty-five specific thematic objectives valid for the entire duration of the legislative term, regularly monitored through official publications that associate individual measures with different thematic areas. ### Economic and financial priorities for 2027 During 2027, the Federal Council's agenda will see the adoption of major legislative and financial acts intended to influence Switzerland's economic framework. Among the planned interventions, the adoption of the dispatch concerning the promotion of the economic hub for the 2028-2031 quadrennium stands out, a strategic document whose stated purpose is to further increase the country's attractiveness for investments and businesses. In the same year, the Government will make fundamental decisions regarding financial indicators relating to the large-scale multi-year financial decrees that will characterize the next legislative term, thereby defining the margins of maneuver for the federal public budget.
### Infrastructure, transport and social reforms Another key sector affected by the 2027 planning is transport, with the planned approval of the Transport '45 dispatch. This measure aims to promote targeted, coordinated and efficient development of the national railway network, the road network and agglomeration traffic. In the social security and welfare sector, the Federal Council will adopt despatches relating to reforms of major institutional and social significance, namely the old-age and survivors' insurance reform known as OASI 2030 and the integration reform. These measures will directly affect the future balances of the Swiss welfare system and the management of social benefits at the federal level.
### Security, agriculture and climate policy The 2027 program also includes major interventions on the front of internal and international security, emergency management and environmental sustainability. The Government intends to adopt the Strategy against domestic, sexual and gender-based violence and proceed with the update of Switzerland's Strategy for the fight against terrorism. To strengthen international cooperation and the capacity to react to unpredictable events, the adoption of the dispatch on Switzerland's accession to the Union Civil Protection Mechanism is planned. On the agricultural and environmental front, the Agricultural Policy 2030+ dispatch will legally define the framework conditions of agricultural policy for an eight-year period, while the revision of the CO2 Act will define Swiss climate policy for the period after 2030, charting the Confederation's ecological course for decades to come.

The periodic publication called Federal Council Objectives constitutes the official reference tool to verify the progress of individual measures associated with the various federal departments.
### Consultation of official documentation Complete documentation presented by the President of the Confederation Guy Parmelin to the Council of States can be consulted through the official channels of the Confederation. item.title: RUAG reorganizes: up to 49 jobs at risk
item.description: The RUAG armament group announces a reorganization that could result in the elimination of up to 49 jobs in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Up to 49 jobs at risk - Involved the sites of Bern, Thun and Emmen - Final decision expected after 6 October - Employee Ready Social Plan
## Key facts - Company: RUAG - Posts at risk: Up to 49 - Sites involved: Bern, Thun, Emmen - Consultation deadline: 6 October
A reorganization of the RUAG armament group could result in the elimination of up to 49 jobs in Switzerland. The news emerged from a statement published by the company on Tuesday. The measure announced by the armament group will specifically affect the Bern, Thun and Emmen sites. The business decision responds to the needs of internal restructuring and adaptation of operational capabilities to current market conditions and the situation of orders in the defense and federal technology sector.
### The production sites involved in the measurement The Thun site, located in the Canton of Bern, is the most affected within the Business Area Ground. In this specific location, up to 24 jobs could be cut due to the lack of new orders. The internal analyses carried out by the company show that current production capacities are not sufficiently exploited, making it necessary to review local staff and operating structures to avoid long-term structural inefficiencies in the terrestrial production sector. ### The outsourcing of IT services In addition to production cuts and the lack of orders in the Ground sector, the reorganisation of the armament group also involves targeted interventions in other strategic departments. In particular, some functions in the IT service will be outsourced with the stated aim of increasing the overall efficiency of company structures. Several operational and IT support activities should be entrusted to specialized external suppliers, with a particular focus on collaboration with the Federal Office of Information Technology and Telecommunications.
### The territorial distribution of IT cuts This second phase of intervention related to IT and administrative efficiency will have repercussions on several locations. In detail, in Thun and Bern a maximum of eight total jobs could be eliminated, while in the Emmen headquarters, located in the Canton of Lucerne, the maximum number of job positions challenged stands at nine units. Overall, the plan affects several technical support and administration functions, redesigning the perimeter of the activities carried out directly within the group compared to those delegated to external and federal bodies.

item.title: Flu vaccines in Switzerland: 40% arrive late
item.description: Delayed deliveries of 40% of flu vaccines in Switzerland. Pharmasuisse runs for cover with a second window at the end of November.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - 40% of vaccines delayed - Two out of four products facing issues - National week confirmed for November - New vaccination window at the end of November
## Key facts - What: Delay in flu vaccine deliveries - Percentage: 40% of doses destined for Switzerland - Products involved: Two out of four - Main period: First week of November - Sponsoring body: Pharmasuisse
40% of the flu vaccines destined for Switzerland will not be available for the population within the originally scheduled times. This supply delay situation will also directly affect Ticino, although without endangering the overall availability of the necessary doses in the canton and nationwide during the cold season. Just a few weeks before the official launch of the seasonal prevention campaign, two of the four products used in the country are experiencing supply issues and will not be present in sufficient quantities for the national vaccination week, scheduled for the beginning of November.
### Supply issues and impact on the territory
Logistical difficulties affect the distribution channels of two of the four pharmaceutical solutions regularly used in Switzerland for immunization against seasonal flu. This temporary reduction in available quantities at the start of the campaign has made an immediate logistical reorganization necessary by trade associations to avoid prolonged inconvenience for citizens wishing to get vaccinated promptly before winter. ### Pharmasuisse's response and new time windows
To cope with the logistical critical issues reported by manufacturers, Pharmasuisse has decided to significantly expand the period dedicated to administering the protective doses. The national vaccination week remains confirmed for the first week of November, as per the initial schedule established by health authorities and trade associations in the pharmaceutical and medical sectors.
However, to compensate for delivery delays and ensure everyone has access to the vaccine without queues or sudden shortages, the organizations have established the opening of an additional time window at the end of November. During this supplementary period, people will be able to go and receive the administration both in authorized pharmacies and, of course, at traditional medical practices throughout the Swiss and Ticino territory.
### Constant monitoring and institutional collaboration
This extraordinary measure will serve to distribute access to vaccination over a longer period of time for the entire resident population. Some operational disruptions related to the management of reservations and user flows are expected in Ticino as well, but at present, no problems of such a magnitude as to compromise the overall success of the health prevention campaign are emerging. Furthermore, the association intends to closely monitor the evolution of the distribution situation, also in view of future winter seasons, to prevent similar logistical bottlenecks in the pharmaceutical supply chain.

In the coming months and years, category organizations will continue to closely monitor the stock situation and supply flows. The managers will remain in constant contact with both pharmaceutical manufacturers and the Federal Office of Public Health and other associations involved in the health sector, so that they can react promptly to any further variation or criticality in the medicines logistics chain.
For its part, the Federal Office of Public Health has not yet issued any official statements regarding these delays in supplies. Citizens interested in undergoing flu vaccination can check in advance the availability of doses at their trusted pharmacy or their treating doctor, taking into account the new end of November window introduced by Pharmasuisse to facilitate access to prophylaxis.

item.title: SNB, 0.0% lead rates: UBS forecasts possible increases
item.description: The Swiss National Bank is expected to keep the lead rate at 0.0% but the risks of an early rise are growing according to UBS.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - SNB policy rate at 0.0% for several months - Growing risk of an increase according to UBS - Key SNB meeting scheduled for September 24 - Forecast for a 25 basis point hike in June 2027
## Key facts - Institution: SNB Swiss National Bank - Analyst bank: UBS led by Sergio Ermotti - Current policy rate: 0.0% - Next SNB meeting: September 24 - Expected hike: 25 basis points or 0.25 points - Expected date for the hike in the baseline scenario: June 2027
The Swiss National Bank (SNB) is expected to keep its policy rate at 0.0% for several more months, but the risk of an increase is growing according to an analysis released by UBS experts. The institution led by Sergio Ermotti published an update today in light of the latest economic and financial developments affecting the Swiss landscape. Currently, according to the bank's assessments, the benchmark rate will not undergo immediate changes. In the forecasts formulated by analysts, the SNB will keep its rate unchanged at the meeting scheduled for September 24. Specialists point out that currently neither recorded inflation nor economic activity justifies a rapid increase in the cost of money in the short term.
### Analysis of future scenarios
In the medium term, the baseline scenario outlined by the bank's specialists continues to forecast a rate increase of 25 basis points, corresponding to 0.25 percentage points, to be placed in June 2027. However, the progression of oil and natural gas prices, combined with the weakening of the franc, could push the central bank to a faster intervention than previously anticipated. The latest economic developments significantly increase the probability of an anticipated intervention and further subsequent adjustments by the SNB, modifying national financial prospects. The dynamics related to the decisions of the Swiss National Bank directly influence the national economic context and the financial prospects of residents and businesses in Switzerland. When referring to reference rates at 0.0%, the effects rapidly extend to credit markets, financing costs for companies, and the conditions of loans and mortgages. The monetary stability guaranteed so far by the central institution has made it possible to contain the pressure on the cost of living and household fixed expenses, but the risk factors highlighted by UBS analysts require constant monitoring of macroeconomic evolution.
### Economic Pressure Factors
The evolution of energy commodity prices, such as oil and natural gas, historically represents one of the main drivers of inflationary pressures within the Swiss market. When these costs increase on international markets, the SNB is called upon to evaluate monetary countermeasures to preserve purchasing power and domestic price stability. Added to this is the variable linked to the trend of the Swiss franc exchange rate. A potential weakening of the Swiss currency against major foreign currencies tends to import inflation through the rising cost of goods purchased abroad, reducing the central institution's room for maneuver and making an earlier hike in interest rates previously planned for the medium term more likely.

item.title: Too big to fail: Council of States discusses UBS rules
item.description: Regulation for too big to fail institutes is at the heart of the parliamentary debate. The RLP proposes to entrust the rules to the Federal Council.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Discussion scheduled within the Council of States - FDP proposal to send the issue back to the Federal Council - Initiative put forward by Andrea Caroni (FDP/AR) - Support from the FDP group and favorable intentions from the Centre
## Key facts What: Too-big-to-fail regulation Where: Council of States When: Thursday (discussion scheduled) Who: Andrea Caroni and FDP councillors Institution involved: UBS
Regulation of banking institutions defined as too big to fail is returning to the center of institutional attention at the federal level. According to the political agenda, the issue regarding the equity capital that UBS will have to hold was scheduled to be discussed on Thursday within the Council of States. However, the handling of the matter could undergo substantial changes following the position taken by the FDP Council of States members. During preliminary meetings, the parliamentary group in fact opted not to address the substance of the issue, preferring to return the entire dossier directly to the Federal Council.
### The FDP parliamentary initiative The political impetus behind this direction bears the signature of Andrea Caroni, representative of the Free Democratic Party for the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. The proposal put forward by Caroni aims to transfer to the Federal Executive the mandate to define and structure the new regulatory provisions on equity capital. In statements reported by national media, the politician highlighted how this path would make it possible to quickly arrive at a clear and legally valid solution, preventing Parliament from having to operate directly as a legislator of specific ordinances in a matter so delicate for the financial stability of the Confederation. The line drawn by the Liberal exponent quickly gathered the compact consensus of the FDP group within the chamber of cantons, also finding favorable openness among the ranks of The Centre party, oriented toward supporting the same institutional approach in view of the formal steps planned in the parliamentary proceedings. ### Historical competencies and regulatory process Andrea Caroni's intervention emphasized the distribution of institutional competencies within the Swiss legal system. As pointed out by the parliamentarian, provisions concerning the own funds of systematically important banking institutions have historically always fallen within the remit of the Federal Council. Historically, these regulatory parameters have been approved through the instrument of the executive ordinance, a procedural path that does not provide for the use of the popular referendum instrument. For proponents of this approach, keeping the matter under the direct responsibility of the Executive represents the most legally straightforward and efficient way also to address the current situation regarding capital requirements applied to large banks.
### The debate on capital requirements and committee compromises The regulatory framework discussed at the federal level is part of a reform context aimed at preventing systemic crises and protecting the country's overall economic stability. The original draft prepared by the Federal Council establishes that UBS must fully cover foreign shareholdings through first-tier core equity, known as CET-1. Faced with this imposition, which is considered particularly rigid, the Committee for Economy and Royalties of the Council of States sought to mediate at the end of August by formulating a compromise proposal. This intermediate solution provides that the coverage of foreign shareholdings does not take place entirely through CET-1 capital, but that half of this amount can be met through the use of so-called AT1 bonds, named Additional Tier 1. The contrast between the Executive's rigorous line and the flexibility hypotheses developed by the parliamentary commission constitutes the central core of the ongoing political confrontation in Bern.

Industry experts and economic analysts continue to closely monitor the evolution of the institutional debate, evaluating the impact that the various foreign asset financing options could generate on the bank's capital structure and its global competitive capacity. The choice between the full coverage model using superior-quality Common Equity Tier 1 and the mixed solution that integrates subordinated debt instruments such as AT1 bonds involves complex assessments involving supervisory authorities, shareholders, and creditors.

item.title: BAK Economics: GDP 2026 at +1.8%, possible rate hike
item.description: The Rhenish institute raises its growth estimate to 1.8% and expects the SNB to intervene as early as December.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - BAK Economics raises the 2026 GDP forecast to 1.8% (from 0.8%). - Inflation forecast for 2026 at 0.6%, 2027 at 0.8%. - Possible increase in SNB interest rates as early as December. - 2027 growth revised downward to 1.3%.
## Key facts - Institution: BAK Economics (Renish institute) - 2026 GDP forecast: 1.8% - Previous 2026 GDP forecast: 0.8% - Q2 2026 growth: 1.5% - 2027 GDP forecast: 1.3% - Inflation 2026: 0.6% - Inflation 2027: 0.8%
### The revision of economic forecasts
The experts at the Renish institute BAK Economics have significantly raised their forecasts for Swiss economic growth this year. According to a press release issued on August 18, 2025, gross domestic product (GDP) will grow by 1.8% in 2026, excluding the impact of sporting events. This figure represents a major adjustment compared to the previously forecasted 0.8%. The primary reason, explained by BAK, lies in the surprisingly positive data regarding economic expansion in the second quarter, which recorded a +1.5% increase compared to the first half of the year.
For 2027, the Basel-based specialists have instead lowered their forecast from 1.4% to 1.3%. The strong dynamics recorded in 2026 are partly attributable to anticipation effects related to U.S. customs policy. However, economists remain cautious due to geopolitical uncertainties and the conflict in the Middle East. 'Planning security, which is essential for investments, has not improved substantially,' reads the official statement from the institute.
On the price front, BAK maintains the inflation forecast for 2026 at 0.6%. For 2027, the estimate has been slightly increased from 0.7% to 0.8%. These data indicate a moderate price stability that, while subdued, provides a clearer reference framework compared to periods of greater volatility. The Swiss National Bank (SNB) could adjust monetary policy in response to this more robust economic environment. ### Implications for Monetary Policy and Investments
The economic outlook described by BAK Economics has direct repercussions on the decisions of the Swiss National Bank (SNB). Despite inflation remaining low, the firmer Swiss economic situation and the clearly positive return of price increases have altered the framework for monetary policy. According to the institute, it is likely that the SNB will raise interest rates as early as December. However, this adjustment to the policy rate should not be interpreted as the beginning of a classic monetary tightening cycle. It would rather be a normalization measure, necessary to align interest rates with the new economic reality.
For Swiss workers and families, this dynamic reflects on the cost of living and financial planning. Inflation at 0.6% in 2026 and 0.8% in 2027 suggests that the erosion of purchasing power will be contained, but not absent. Wages, often linked to collective labor agreements, may not adjust immediately to these changes, requiring careful management of household budgets. Companies, on the other hand, face challenges related to planning security, a fundamental element for investments that, according to BAK, has not substantially improved.
### Comparison Between Previous and Current Forecasts
The revision of the forecasts highlights a significant change in direction. The shift from a projected growth of 0.8% to 1.8% for 2026 signals an unexpected economic acceleration. This improvement was driven primarily by the second quarter, with an increase of 1.5%. In contrast, the forecast for 2027 has fallen from 1.4% to 1.3%, indicating a moderation of future growth. This asymmetry suggests that the stimulating effect of recent data may not be sustainable in the long term without further supporting factors.
American trade policy plays a crucial role in this analysis. The anticipation effects recorded in 2026 could be exhausted in 2027, contributing to the slight decline in the growth forecast. Furthermore, geopolitical uncertainties and the conflict in the Middle East continue to weigh on investor expectations. For savers, this means that diversification of investments and prudence in risk management remain essential strategies in a context of persistent volatility.

item.description: The OECD released the report on Switzerland appreciating economic resilience but calling for reforms in health, welfare and administration by the end of 2027.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The OECD published its report on Switzerland on September 15, 2026 - The country's economic policy and resilience were praised - Reforms were requested in healthcare, pensions, and administration
## Key facts - Publication date: September 15, 2026 - Issuing body: OECD - Subject of analysis: Switzerland's economic policy - Reform horizon: Long-term - Growth report deadline: End of 2027
On September 15, 2026, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development published its report on Switzerland, expressing appreciation for the country's economic policy approach. In light of multiple challenges, however, the OECD believes that action is necessary to ensure Switzerland's long-term competitiveness and innovative capacity. item.title: OECD sees more growth in Switzerland, GDP 2026 at 2.0%
item.description: The OECD revises upwards the forecasts for Switzerland: GDP growth to 2.0% in 2026 and stable average inflation to 0.6%.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Growth forecasts raised to 2% for 2026 - Average inflation expected at 0.6% this year and next - Domestic demand identified as the growth engine
## Key facts - Organization: OECD - 2026 Growth: 2.0% - Previous 2026 Growth: 1.1% - 2027 Growth: 1.4% - Previous 2027 Growth: 1.5% - Average inflation: 0.6% - Previous inflation: 0.7% - Source: ATS
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development has sharply revised upwards its growth forecasts for the Swiss economy in 2026, bringing them to 2.0% and marking a significant departure from the 1.1% previously indicated in June. This improvement in economic prospects reflects the more robust economic trend recorded during the second quarter, according to the Economic Survey published today. Regarding the following year, 2027, the estimate has instead been slightly lowered to 1.4% compared to the previous 1.5%. It should be noted that this estimate is not adjusted for sporting events. On the price increase front, average inflation is expected at 0.6% for both the current year and the next, marking a slight decrease compared to the 0.7% previously forecasted by official data. The publication describes Switzerland as a stable, prosperous, and dynamic economy, capable of absorbing recent shocks relatively favorably. Price inflation has remained at subdued levels partly due to the low energy intensity that characterizes the country. Despite these positive elements, some structural and cyclical challenges identified by the Paris-based international body remain. Domestic demand continues to represent the main engine of Swiss economic growth, while external demand must contend with several critical issues.
### Pressures on external demand and exports
The released data highlight how global uncertainty, higher energy prices, and recent tariffs imposed on Swiss products continue to weigh significantly on external demand. This scenario puts all export-oriented companies to the test, as they must navigate a complex international context characterized by growing barriers. However, the structural solidity of the national economy has helped cushion the blows resulting from these geopolitical and commercial tensions. Authorities and economic operators are closely monitoring the evolution of foreign markets, especially regarding the Confederation's traditional trading partners. The international organization suggests in this regard to expand relations with existing partners and open new outlet markets to diversify commercial risk and support the long-term competitiveness of Swiss companies, thus ensuring greater overall resilience of the national economic system in the coming years. ## Practical analysis of economic policy recommendations
The indications provided by the international organization offer significant food for thought for the future management of the Confederation's economic and fiscal policy. On the economic policy front, the institution recommends safeguarding the solid public finances that have always characterized the country in the long term. Among the options suggested to achieve this goal are higher revenues, which could be obtained for example through VAT, the implementation of targeted budget savings, and the achievement of a healthcare system characterized by greater efficiency. However, the need for structural reforms does not only concern the state budget, but extends to other key sectors for the well-being of the community and the stability of the Swiss economic system.
### Structural reforms and old-age provision
Among the sectors indicated as priorities for the introduction of reforms are old-age provision and the construction sector. The sustainability of the pension system represents a crucial challenge for the future, given demographic trends and the increase in life expectancy of the resident population. At the same time, the construction sector requires targeted interventions to maintain its efficiency and respond to the country's housing and infrastructure needs. Regarding the regulation of the banking sector, the international body explicitly invites strengthening financial stability, while paying attention not to excessively compromise the attractiveness of the Swiss financial center at an international level. The balance between regulatory rigor and global competitiveness remains an absolute priority for the supervisory authorities and the federal government, called upon to protect the sector from systemic risks without stifling innovation and private investment.

To consciously deal with economic dynamics, assess the impact of price fluctuations and optimise the management of your financial and social security resources, it is advisable to rely on the analysis tools available online.

## In brief - **Perimeter**: Ticino and Italian provinces CO, VA and VB. - **Ticino directory**: 207 records from the official list. - **Italian directory**: 542 records filtered to the three border provinces. - **Verified duty**: regional sources for Mendrisiotto, Luganese, Bellinzonese, Biasca e Valli, Locarnese.
A guide to checking the current source in the right canton, without inventing calendars or turning a link into an opening promise. ## What is verified and what is not The verified duty data published by our dataset concerns five Ticino regions: Mendrisiotto, Luganese, Bellinzonese, Biasca e Valli and Locarnese. Locarnese uses a regional association source; for other cantons we provide navigable official links where available, but publish no unified roster, active coverage or inferred hours.
Open the cantonal or provincial source before travelling, follow its published instructions and call the pharmacy. Where a source exposes no public feed or roster, the guide says so rather than filling the gap with assumptions.
## Directory, opening hours and duty: three different data points - **directory**: A directory record means that the official catalogue contains the entry; it does not mean that the pharmacy is open now. - **opening hours**: Opening hours are shown only when the page or source publishes them; they are not inferred from the directory or its timestamp. - **verified duty**: Verified duty means a regional interval published by OFCT or the relevant association source; it is not the same as continuous opening. Check by phone before travelling. ## Scope, sources and timestamp This guide uses separate snapshots: a Ticino address directory, a filtered Italian directory and a regional duty dataset (OFCT and the Locarnese association source). The sources are not merged into one opening status.
- **Official Ticino pharmacy list**: 207 records, retrieved at 2026-09-14T10:03:57.824Z. [official list](https://www4.ti.ch/fileadmin/DSS/DSP/UFC/PDF/Elenchi_e_Indirizzi/Lista_Farmacie.pdf) - **Official Italian dataset filtered to provinces CO, VA and VB**: 542 records, retrieved at 2026-09-14T10:03:57.824Z. [OFCT source](https://www.ofct.ch/farmacieturno/)
**Latest snapshot retrieval**: directories 2026-09-14T10:03:57.824Z; duty 2026-09-15T09:40:29.571Z. The timestamp records when the source snapshot was retrieved; it is not an opening time and does not prove that a pharmacy is open now.
This is not nationwide coverage: the perimeter is limited to Ticino and the Italian provinces CO, VA and VB. Locarnese is included as the fifth duty region through the regional association source farmacielocarnese.ch. Its interval is published only after a unique match with the cantonal directory; the source does not replace the directory. For Locarnese: regional association source [farmacielocarnese.ch](https://www.farmacielocarnese.ch/); the parser publishes an interval only after a unique Farmacia-and-locality match with the cantonal directory and copies no address from the source. No Italian on-duty claim is made: the Italian catalogue is an address directory and does not prove that a pharmacy is open or on duty.

item.title: Adult education increases income 50%
item.description: UST Study: Achieving Secondary Title II in Adulthood Leads to +50% Income and Employment at 80%
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Adult secondary II qualification increases income by 50% - NEET share drops from 20% to 11% - Employed rise to 80%
## Key facts - Institution: Federal Statistical Office (FSO) - Period: 2013-2023 (10 years) - Sample: 11,000 people - Types of qualifications: AFC (84%), CFP (14%) - Initial income: CHF 3,500/month - Final income: CHF 5,200/month - Income increase: 50%
NEUCHÂTEL - Obtaining a secondary II level qualification significantly improves the labour market situation and income, even though it occurs only in adulthood, according to a detailed analysis published by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO).
According to the study, Neuchâtel specialists considered the nearly 11,000 people who in 2018 obtained a Federal Certificate of Practical Training (CFP), a Federal Certificate of Capacity (AFC), a general culture certificate or a high school diploma at age 25 or older. These qualifications correspond to the completion of secondary II level education.
Five years earlier, in 2013, only 60% of these individuals were active in the labour market and one in five (20%) was neither employed nor in education or training (NEET). Moreover, for employed persons the gross labour income was "low", averaging CHF 3,500 per month. This scenario poses a significant challenge for the Swiss labour market and social security systems such as AVS/AHV, as few people without adequate training contribute less to the system.
Five years after obtaining the qualification, in 2023, the NEET share had almost halved (11%) and the share of employed persons increased "substantially", reaching nearly 80%. These figures are comparable to those of the population in the same age bracket, demonstrating that adult education can effectively bridge the employment gap.
### Types of students The characteristics of this adult population, composed of 45% women, are highly heterogeneous: it may include people who were already in Switzerland at age 15 and who, after age 25, obtained their first qualification (20%) or an additional secondary II level qualification (38%), as well as recent immigrants already holding a qualification of this level (12%), or people without post‑compulsory education coming from the kindergarten sector (6%). The UST analysis shows that the economic impact of adult education translates into a significant increase in average income, which rose from 3,500 to 5,200 Swiss francs per month, an increase of about 50% over ten years. This rise in purchasing power has positive effects on the cost of living in Switzerland, allowing these individuals to contribute more to the national economy and to meet daily expenses with greater financial stability.
Overall, 84% obtained a Federal Certificate of Capacity (AFC) and 14% a Federal Certificate of Practical Training (CFP). The latter, lasting two years, is aimed at young people who have mainly practical skills; the AFC, lasting three or four years, includes a broader theoretical component and a larger number of tasks compared to the CFP. These professional qualifications represent a concrete opportunity to improve one's position in the Swiss labour market, where continuous training is often a decisive factor for professional growth.
### Different training paths The group of people who arrived in Switzerland after completing compulsory schooling, for whom the secondary level II qualification is the first post‑compulsory credential they obtain, stood out for a particularly high percentage of CFP (35%). This proportion even reaches 66% for people coming from the kindergarten sector, the UST notes. These data highlight how training paths in Switzerland can adapt to the various needs and backgrounds of participants, offering opportunities for professional re‑placement and social integration.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). The UST study shows that investing in training as an adult is an effective strategy to improve one's position in the Swiss labour market. For those who wish to undertake this path, it is essential to know the requirements and procedures necessary to access these training courses. The competent cantonal administrations offer detailed information on the specific requirements for each type of degree, such as the federal certificate of ability (AFC) or the federal certificate of practical training (CFP).
### Procedure for access to training The first step is an assessment of your skills and professional goals. Next, you should contact the vocational training centers or schools that offer the desired pathways. Many cantons organize evening or part-time courses designed specifically for working adults, allowing study and professional activity to be reconciled. It is important to consider that vocational training in Switzerland often involves costs that can be partially covered by scholarships or subsidies, especially for disadvantaged people.
For those wishing to deepen vocational training opportunities in Switzerland, the Swiss Centre for Vocational Training, Career, University and Career Guidance Service at www.orientamento.ch provides detailed information on the available pathways.
Evaluating a Ticino job offer? Simulate your [net payslip](nav:payslip): enter gross salary, marital status and municipality for a detailed breakdown.

item.title: LAMal premium increases: the policy rebounds responsibilities
item.description: The annual increases in LAMal premiums are punctual, with the policy rebounding responsibilities between the Confederation and the Cantons. The cost affects the quality of life of Swiss families.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Annual increases in LAMal premiums are as punctual as the seasons. - Politics bounces responsibility between the Confederation and the Cantons. - Proposal: make health insurance premiums tax-deductible. - The cost conditions the quality of life for Swiss families.
## Key facts - Problem: Continuous increase in mandatory health insurance premiums. - Responsibility: Bounces between federal, cantonal, hospitals, and insurance funds. - Impact: A cost that conditions rent, taxes, and daily spending. - Proposal: Full deductibility of premiums from taxes.
### The mechanism of institutional bouncing Every year, with the punctuality of the seasons, come the increases in mandatory health insurance premiums. With them come the explanations, justifications, and the political refrain: 'It is not up to us', 'We cannot do anything'. It is a mechanism that repeats cyclically, where competencies pass from one institutional level to another without the final bill changing its recipient.
Healthcare is a topic that explodes, but politics seems incapable of intervening on the deep causes. The debate often focuses on who is responsible: the Confederation, the Cantons, hospitals, doctors, or health insurance funds. In reality, while responsibilities bounce around, the economic weight always falls on the pockets of citizens. For many Swiss families, the premium is no longer a simple budget item, but a cost that directly impacts the quality of life, on par with rent, mortgage, taxes, energy, and transport.
The paradox is evident: there is continuous talk of cost containment, reforms, and efficiency. However, premiums increase punctually, and citizens are asked to tighten their belts. The serious question is not whether healthcare costs money, but why it costs so much and why no one truly intervenes on the causes, such as bureaucracy, duplicate structures, or inefficiencies. The citizen becomes the last link in the chain, paying premiums, taxes, and deductibles, sometimes giving up on care due to the high cost. Yet, the public reaction often prevails in silence and resignation, accustomed to the idea that nothing can be done, when instead there are immediate measures to consider. [Other articles on LAMal](nav:health) ### Analysis of System Responsibilities and Inefficiencies The original text highlights a structural fragility of the Swiss healthcare system: the separation between defining competencies and assuming economic responsibility. When it comes to health, blame tends to be fragmented among multiple actors. The Confederation manages federal aspects, the Cantons local ones, but hospitals, doctors, and health insurance funds also contribute to cost trends. This fragmentation prevents a unified intervention on the main causes of healthcare inflation.
There are concrete questions that politics should address transparently. Which services can be rationalized? How much do bureaucracy, duplicated structures, and special interests impact system inefficiencies? Currently, the system seems to continuously generate new costs, but there is a lack of willingness to intervene at the root. This creates a sense of powerlessness in citizens, who perceive a lack of concrete protection. Citizens pay several times: premiums, taxes, deductibles, and co-payments. This multiplication of fiscal and contributory burdens weighs on purchasing power and limits families' economic freedom of choice.
The public reaction to these increases is described as strangely weak. Marginal details are discussed for weeks, people get indignant about minor issues, but when faced with a problem affecting the budget of hundreds of thousands of people every year, resignation and silence prevail. People have become accustomed to increases, explanations, and the shifting of responsibilities. This habituation to the unacceptable is perhaps the real problem blocking change. It is not enough to accept that healthcare costs money; it is necessary to demand clarity on where the money is spent and who is accountable. The absence of a single, identifiable responsible party makes it difficult to exercise democratic control over healthcare spending. [Cost of Living Comparison](nav:cost-of-living)
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Concrete proposal: tax deductibility of premiums The source proposes a concrete and immediately applicable measure to alleviate the burden of increases: making mandatory health insurance premiums fully tax-deductible. This solution would not solve the root problem, nor would it reduce overall healthcare costs, nor would it replace necessary structural reforms. However, it would have an immediate effect: it would reduce the tax burden on families and citizens, returning to them a portion of what they are currently forced to allocate to mandatory coverage. The central argument is simple: we wouldn't want to tax the same income twice, would we? If healthcare costs increase, deductibility would partially offset this increase, maintaining more purchasing power in the hands of taxpayers.
For residents in Switzerland, this measure would require careful verification in their tax declaration. It is crucial to assess how the deduction would integrate with current deductions for medical expenses and deductibles. Since federal direct tax and cantonal taxes operate on separate levels, the impact of deductibility varies depending on the canton and overall income. Citizens should consult their declaration to verify how healthcare expenses are already treated and if a regulatory change would bring a significant net benefit.
While awaiting potential legislative reforms, citizens can still optimize their current tax situation. It is advisable to check if one is entitled to cantonal subsidies for premium reduction, which can cover part of the cost. Furthermore, it is useful to compare offers from different health insurance providers ('cassa malati') to ensure being on the most advantageous plan possible. To accurately calculate how much tax is actually paid and how healthcare expenses affect taxable income, a specific tool is available. [Salary and Tax Calculator](nav:calculator)
*Source: [tio.ch](https://www.tio.ch/rubriche/ospite/1950107/premi-politica-continua-responsabilita-salute)*

item.description: The SRG starts the Enavant project to cut 270 million francs by 2029, with 80 million by 2027. 20% reduction in managers and stop in the Champions League.
item.content:encoded:
## In breve - Risparmi SSR: 270 milioni CHF entro il 2029 - Taglio dirigenti: oltre il 20% a livello dirigenziale - SRF: meno 9,7 milioni e 38 posti di lavoro - UEFA Champions League: stop alle dirette dal 2027/28
## Fatti chiave Società: Società svizzera di radiotelevisione (SSR) Progetto: Trasformazione aziendale Enavant Obiettivo risparmio: 270 milioni di franchi entro il 2029 Risparmio 2027: 80 milioni di franchi Riduzione posti dirigenziali: oltre il 20% rispetto al 2024 Risparmio SRF: 9,7 milioni di franchi entro il 2027 Posti di lavoro persi SRF: 38 a tempo pieno entro il 2027 Stop UEFA Champions League: dalla stagione 2027/2028
La Società svizzera di radiotelevisione (SSR), nell’ambito del suo progetto di trasformazione aziendale denominato Enavant, ha delineato lunedì le misure di risparmio previste per il 2027. La decisione del Consiglio federale di ridurre il canone radiotelevisivo impone alla SSR di tagliare circa 270 milioni di franchi entro il 2029, con una prima tranche di 80 milioni da raggiungere già entro il 2027. La strategia di risparmio mira a salvaguardare il programma offerto al pubblico, concentrando circa il 95% delle economie su strutture, processi e modalità di produzione, come comunicato lo scorso giugno.
La SSR sta implementando un nuovo modello organizzativo, con la definizione quasi completa dei tre livelli dirigenziali più elevati. A questi livelli, si registrerà una riduzione di oltre il 20% delle posizioni direttive rispetto ai dati del 2024. Queste misure di razionalizzazione avranno inevitabilmente ripercussioni sul personale. Una parte della riduzione dei posti di lavoro sarà gestita attraverso la fluttuazione naturale e i pensionamenti, applicando il piano sociale della SSR per i dipendenti interessati.
Susanne Wille, direttrice generale della SSR, ha sottolineato l'impegno verso il pubblico: "Siamo impegnati nei confronti del nostro pubblico. Per questo attuiamo il mandato di risparmio politico assicurando che il canone radiotelevisivo vada il più possibile a beneficio del programma. A tale scopo, mettiamo in discussione in modo coerente anche le nostre strutture: ai livelli dirigenziali più alti riduciamo di oltre il 20% le posizioni direttive. Allo stesso tempo, proteggiamo il programma ovunque sia possibile". Ha aggiunto che questi cambiamenti, sebbene impegnativi per l'azienda e i collaboratori, sono necessari per rendere la SSR più digitale, efficiente e agile, garantendo così un servizio pubblico forte anche in futuro.
Le ulteriori misure di trasformazione e di risparmio per gli anni 2028 e 2029 verranno definite gradualmente nei diversi settori e regioni, seguendo la pianificazione finanziaria. La SSR continuerà ad adattare, sviluppare e rinnovare la propria offerta di programmi nei prossimi anni.
### SRF e le sue ripercussioni
All'interno di SRF (Schweizer Radio und Fernsehen), entro il 2027 sono previste economie per 9,7 milioni di franchi, con la conseguente eliminazione di 38 posti di lavoro a tempo pieno. Le misure di risparmio toccheranno sia i programmi televisivi che quelli radiofonici, interessando tutte le unità di offerta: informazione, cultura, società e conoscenza, e intrattenimento, nonché la distribuzione regionale. Circa la metà dei tagli di personale avverrà tramite fluttuazioni naturali. Le modifiche al palinsesto televisivo impatteranno diversi programmi. The decisions announced by the SSR, although focused on internal reorganization and savings, carry practical implications that deserve thorough analysis, especially concerning public service and the offering aimed at the Swiss public. The reduction of the radio and television licence fee, imposed by the Federal Council, acts as a catalyst for these measures, forcing the SSR to undertake a deep review of its structures and processes. The stated objective of preserving programme quality, by concentrating cuts on organizational and productive aspects rather than editorial content, represents a complex challenge.
The 20% reduction in managerial positions at the top of the company signals a willingness to streamline the hierarchical structure and, potentially, to increase decision‑making efficiency. This, combined with the management of savings through natural fluctuation and retirements, aims to mitigate the direct social impact on employees, although the need for further measures in the future cannot be ruled out entirely. The SSR must balance the need for economic efficiency with the maintenance of a public‑service mandate that covers a wide range of interests and audience segments.
### Impact on offering and consumption
The repercussions on programme offerings, in particular those announced for SRF, highlight a trend towards greater digitalization and a focus on streaming and digital platforms. The concentration of weekly radio formats to the 40 weeks of the year with the highest impact, and the broadcasting of repeats or music programmes during less strategic periods, suggests a rationalisation of resources devoted to radio production. This could lead to a reduced variety of original content in certain periods of the year, an aspect that regular listeners might notice.
The planned close collaboration between the cultural broadcasters of the different linguistic regions (Radio SRF 2 Kultur, RTS Espace 2 and Rete Due) is a sign of integration and potential synergy, aimed at optimising resources and creating a cross‑regional cultural offering. SRF Virus’s orientation towards digital platforms indicates a strategy targeting a younger audience that prefers on‑demand content accessible on mobile devices. This strategic shift reflects global trends in media consumption, but it could marginalise those who are not fully integrated into the digital world.
The renunciation of live broadcasting of UEFA Champions League matches starting with the 2027/2028 season is one of the most striking decisions. The acquisition of sports rights is an ever‑evolving and increasingly costly market. The SSR, like many public broadcasters in Europe, must contend with limited budgets and the need to prioritise investments. The decision to forego an event of such magnitude, although popular, frees resources that can be redirected towards other sectors considered priorities for public service, such as information or culture. This change will oblige football fans to seek alternatives to follow the competition, potentially on paid platforms or other channels not broadcast by the SSR. The SSR is therefore redefining its role and offering in a rapidly transforming media landscape, seeking a balance between financial sustainability, technological innovation and fulfilment of its public‑service mandate. item.title: New electronic health record: ok from the National Council
item.description: The law for the new electronic health record in Switzerland has been approved. It will replace the previous infrastructure by 2030.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The National Council has approved a new health law - The electronic health record (EHR) is born - It will replace the previous computerized patient record - Introduction planned by 2030 by the Federal Council
## Key facts - Votes in favour: 134 - Votes against: 53 - Abstentions: 10 - Restructuring deadline: by 2030 - Management and financing: Cantons
Following the disappointing results of the computerized patient record, defined by many as a genuine fiasco due to a complex structure and a burdensome opening process that held back its use well below expectations, the National Council has decided to give a new impetus to the digitalization of the Swiss healthcare sector. Meeting to debate the future of medical data in the Confederation, the plenum approved a new law aimed at introducing the electronic health record. The dossier now moves to the Council of States for the subsequent legislative stages provided for by the federal legal system.
### Objectives and structure of the digital reform
The bill presented by the government last autumn aims to put the individual at the centre of their clinical history, offering an overview of relevant medical data without any barriers linked to domicile, place of treatment, or specific service provider. Information currently fragmented, including consultation reports, discharge summaries, vaccinations, medications taken, and laboratory values, will be stored and made digitally available in a single place, always accessible. The intent pursued by the Federal Council, as highlighted in the parliamentary debate, is to proceed with a radical restructuring by 2030, replacing the previous infrastructure to globally improve the quality of care, increase patient safety, eliminate duplications, and concretely contribute to containing overall healthcare costs. Many parliamentarians insisted on the need to make up for lost ground, avoiding the design errors that characterized the past. ### Coinvolgimento dei professionisti e modello automatico
A differenza del precedente sistema, la nuova normativa stabilisce che tutti i professionisti della salute dovranno obbligatoriamente partecipare al sistema della cartella sanitaria elettronica. L'obbligo non riguarderà più soltanto gli ospedali e gli istituti di cura, già tenuti a collegarsi, ma verrà esteso a medici, farmacisti, fisioterapisti e a tutti gli altri fornitori di prestazioni ambulatoriali che emettono fatture a carico dell'assicurazione obbligatoria delle cure medico-sanitarie. Questo ampliamento della platea mira a sfruttare appieno il potenziale tecnologico dello strumento digitale raccogliendo un volume di dati clinici completo e omogeneo su tutto il territorio nazionale svizzero.
Un altro aspetto centrale della riforma riguarda le modalità di adesione per la popolazione residente. La cartella elettronica non dovrà essere richiesta attivamente dai singoli cittadini: ogni persona domiciliata in Svizzera la riceverà in modo automatico e totalmente gratuito. Ciononostante, il principio della volontarietà d'uso rimarrà pienamente garantito. Chiunque non desideri disporre della cartella sanitaria elettronica potrà infatti opporsi alla sua apertura iniziale o richiederne la completa eliminazione in qualsiasi momento, avvalendosi della clausola di esclusione volontaria. In questo modo, i pazienti manterranno la piena e incondizionata sovranità sui propri dati personali e clinici, conservando il potere decisionale assoluto su chi potrà accedere alle informazioni e su quali sezioni specifiche consultare.
### Organizzazione centralizzata e competenze cantonali
Sul piano infrastrutturale e organizzativo, la nuova cartella si differenzierà nettamente dalla sua antenata grazie all'adozione di un'architettura centralizzata. Su proposta della commissione preparatoria, è prevista la creazione di un'unica comunità nazionale di riferimento che agirà da interlocutore ufficiale per i titolari della cartella, per i professionisti della salute e per le strutture sanitarie coinvolte. Questa entità centrale sarà gestita e finanziata direttamente dai Cantoni, una soluzione che nel corso della votazione in aula ha superato la proposta alternativa che affidava la medesima responsabilità alla Confederazione. Tale ripartizione di compiti istituzionali sottolinea il ruolo chiave che le autorità cantonali continueranno a svolgere nella governance della sanità pubblica svizzera, coordinando le risorse e l'implementazione pratica del progetto sul proprio territorio.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Security debate and political skepticism
Despite the large majority vote in the National Council, the project was not free from criticism and concerns raised by a parliamentary minority, particularly among the ranks of the Swiss People's Party (SVP). Representatives of this faction, while agreeing on the underlying goals of health improvement, raised strong doubts regarding the clarity of the actual costs of the operation and the security of the model based on automatic exclusion. According to the critical arguments presented in parliament, the approach providing for automatic enrollment unless explicitly opposed amounts to a mechanism where silence is taken as consent on extremely sensitive data, for which it would instead be appropriate to require a prior and explicit expression of intent from the individual.
Also targeted by critics was the choice to focus on a large-scale centralized infrastructure, considered a complex and potentially risky federal IT project. The danger of vulnerabilities to cyberattacks by hackers was highlighted, alongside the possibility of human errors in managing such an extensive system. Health Minister Elisabeth Baume-Schneider responded to these concerns, assuring that data security represents an absolute and unquestionable priority for the executive. The Federal Councillor reiterated the institutional commitment to delivering a technological tool that is fully worthy of citizens' trust, balancing the efficiency of digitization with the rigorous protection of privacy.
### Next institutional steps and further details
The regulatory process for the electronic patient dossier now continues as the dossier moves to the Council of States, where senators will discuss the technical and financial details approved by the National Council. A transition phase thus begins for residents and Swiss healthcare operators toward the 2030 target set by the Federal Council for the completion of the digital reorganization. Those wishing to monitor the evolution of health regulations, assess the impact of fixed costs related to the healthcare system, or learn more about aspects related to LAMal benefits and related coverages can consult the information tools available online, including insights dedicated to the cost of living and fixed expenses in Switzerland. For a comprehensive analysis of monthly expenses and to calculate the impact of mandatory costs on your budget, [consult the cost of living comparator](nav:cost-of-living).

item.description: The electronic health record, the Mercosur agreement and the Swiss agriculture funds have been approved in Parliament.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Approved the electronic health record - Green light to the agreement with Mercosur - Support for Swiss agriculture - New measures on generic drugs
## Key facts - Motion author: Mauro Poggia - Agreement countries: Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay - Agriculture financing: CHF 517 million - Support period: 2028-2033 - Mercosur agreement votes States: 35 in favour, 7 against, 3 abstentions - National health record votes: 134 in favour, 53 against, 10 abstentions
On Monday, the debate opened in the National Council with the new electronic health record, which received the first approval by the Federal Parliament. In the meantime, the Council of States has given the green light to the free trade agreement with the Mercosur countries, granting aid of 517 million francs for the period 2028-2033 aimed at strengthening the competitiveness of farms. These dossiers are part of the great themes that are marking the current legislature together with Bilateral III, UBS's own funds and the increase in VAT for the army. During the parliamentary session, attention focused on several crucial issues for the Swiss economy and health, touching on different areas ranging from international treaties to the digitisation of the national health sector and the management of health costs.
### The debate on generic drugs and the Poggia motion
Another central theme The parliamentary process saw opposing views regarding international treaties and the digitalization of public and healthcare services. Regarding the free trade agreement with Mercosur countries, which includes Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay, the Council of States reiterated its support after the National Council had voted against it last June. The agreement passed to the upper house, receiving 35 votes in favor, 7 against, and 3 abstentions. Along with the trade agreement, the senators approved a financial support package of 517 million francs for the period between 2028 and 2033. This amount is specifically intended to strengthen the competitiveness of Swiss agriculture and sparked extensive discussions in the chamber before reaching a compromise aimed at protecting local producers.
### The reform of the electronic health record and the phasing out of the EPD
On the domestic and healthcare front, the Federal Council's bill concerning the new electronic health record received its first green light from the National Council with 134 votes in favor, 53 against, and 10 abstentions. According to the plans outlined by the federal executive, in the future all residents in Switzerland will automatically and free of charge receive an electronic health record, unless they explicitly opt out. The new federal law will clearly define the tasks and responsibilities belonging to the Confederation and the Cantons, as well as regulate financing methods. This tool is destined to replace the previous patient electronic record, known as the EPD, which over the years has proven to be poorly used. During the plenary discussion, many national councilors highlighted the need not to repeat the mistakes made with the EPD, openly defined by several speakers as a true institutional and managerial fiasco. The old record was based on an overly complex structure, which involved numerous private providers and imposed a burdensome opening process for users. Such bureaucratic and technical obstacles meant that the actual use of the EPD remained well below the initial expectations formulated by the federal authorities.

The ongoing parliamentary session highlights the intention to reorganize several key sectors of public administration and personal services, focusing on greater centralization and stricter cost control. Regarding the future management of the electronic patient dossier, the tool should be administered by a single community commissioned directly by the Cantons. This organizational choice was specifically designed to guarantee a rapid introduction of the system and facilitate its daily management for both citizens and health professionals. In addition to digital aspects, the legislation provides that doctors, pharmacists, physiotherapists, and other outpatient service providers will also be legally required to use the electronic health record as part of their daily professional activity. This obligation aims to create an integrated healthcare ecosystem, reducing duplication of examinations and improving coordination between the various levels of care throughout Swiss territory.
### Procedure and next institutional steps
As Parliament continues its work on the legislature's major dossiers, citizens and economic operators are called upon to monitor the evolution of the regulations approved in recent weeks. Regarding the future reception of the electronic health record, resident individuals will not have to take any immediate action, as distribution will take place automatically according to the deadlines that will be established by the Federal Executive, without prejudice to the right to formally object. Regulatory developments regarding pharmaceutical expenditure and the direct importation of generics will instead require further institutional steps before finding practical application in Swiss pharmacies and hospitals. ## Directory, opening hours and duty: three different data points - **directory**: A directory record means that the official catalogue contains the entry; it does not mean that the pharmacy is open now. - **opening hours**: Opening hours are shown only when the page or source publishes them; they are not inferred from the directory or its timestamp. - **verified duty**: Verified duty means a regional interval published by OFCT or the relevant association source; it is not the same as continuous opening. Check by phone before travelling. ## Scope, sources and timestamp This guide uses separate snapshots: a Ticino address directory, a filtered Italian directory and a regional duty dataset (OFCT and the Locarnese association source). The sources are not merged into one opening status.
- **Official Ticino pharmacy list**: 207 records, retrieved at 2026-09-14T10:03:57.824Z. [official list](https://www4.ti.ch/fileadmin/DSS/DSP/UFC/PDF/Elenchi_e_Indirizzi/Lista_Farmacie.pdf) - **Official Italian dataset filtered to provinces CO, VA and VB**: 542 records, retrieved at 2026-09-14T10:03:57.824Z. [Ministry of Health dataset](https://www.dati.salute.gov.it/it/dataset/farmacie/) - **Regional sources for Ticino duty coverage**: areas Mendrisiotto, Luganese, Bellinzonese, Biasca e Valli, Locarnese, retrieved at 2026-09-15T09:40:29.571Z. [OFCT source](https://www.ofct.ch/farmacieturno/)
**Latest snapshot retrieval**: directories 2026-09-14T10:03:57.824Z; duty 2026-09-15T09:40:29.571Z. The timestamp records when the source snapshot was retrieved; it is not an opening time and does not prove that a pharmacy is open now.
This is not nationwide coverage: the perimeter is limited to Ticino and the Italian provinces CO, VA and VB. Locarnese is included as the fifth duty region through the regional association source farmacielocarnese.ch. Its interval is published only after a unique match with the cantonal directory; the source does not replace the directory. For Locarnese: regional association source [farmacielocarnese.ch](https://www.farmacielocarnese.ch/); the parser publishes an interval only after a unique Farmacia-and-locality match with the cantonal directory and copies no address from the source. No Italian on-duty claim is made: the Italian catalogue is an address directory and does not prove that a pharmacy is open or on duty.

item.title: Why Interest Rates in Switzerland Remain Low
item.description: The SNB has maintained the rate at 0% for over a year; Swiss inflation at 0.8% in August; average 10-year mortgages at 1.9%; next revision on 24 September.
item.content:encoded:
## In breve - BNS lascia il tasso di riferimento allo 0% da oltre un anno. - Inflazione svizzera ad agosto allo 0,8% su base annua. - Mutui a 10 anni in media all’1,9% secondo Comparis.
## Fatti chiave - Tasso di riferimento BNS: 0% - Tasso di riferimento USA (forchetta): 3,5-3,75% - Tasso di riferimento BCE: 2,5% - Inflazione Regno Unito: 2,9% - Inflazione media europea: 2,9% - Inflazione USA: 3,4% - Tasso Giappone: 1% - Mutui ipotecari 10 anni (Comparis): 1,9% - Inflazione Svizzera agosto: 0,8% - Data prossima revisione BNS: 24 settembre
Lead: La Banca nazionale svizzera (BNS) ha mantenuto il suo tasso di interesse di riferimento allo 0,0%, un livello eccezionalmente basso nel panorama globale, in vigore da oltre un anno. Questo rende i prestiti più economici ma lascia i depositi con interessi quasi nulli. La prossima valutazione della BNS è prevista per il 24 settembre. Negli Stati Uniti il tasso di riferimento si colloca nella forchetta del 3,5‑3,75% e la Federal Reserve è attesa per un aumento già questo mercoledì, primo dal 2023, seguito probabilmente da un altro rialzo. La Banca centrale europea (BCE) ha invece portato il tasso dal 2,25 al 2,5% giovedì scorso, mentre la Banca d’Inghilterra rimane al 3,75% e sta rivedendo la propria politica questa settimana. L’inflazione nel Regno Unito è al 2,9%, poco sopra l’obiettivo, così come la media europea (2,9%) e quella statunitense (3,4%). In Giappone il tasso è all’1% e la banca centrale locale dovrebbe aumentarlo di un punto entro fine settimana.
### Implicazioni per il credito e il risparmio Con bassi tassi, chiedere un prestito è vantaggioso, ma il denaro lasciato sui conti bancari rende pochissimo. Secondo Caroline Hilb di Raiffeisen, la situazione deriva dall’inflazione contenuta e dalla forza del franco, oltre dalla rigorosa disciplina del debito svizzera, di cui il freno all’indebitamento è un pilastro. Daniel Kalt di UBS aggiunge che questa disciplina aiuta a limitare il debito pubblico e a evitare sprechi di denaro dei contribuenti.
I mutui ipotecari, tuttavia, mostrano un leggero rialzo: secondo Comparis, quelli a durata decennale sono in media all’1,9%. Hilb sottolinea che questo aumento segue le tendenze internazionali e non è immune agli spostamenti dei tassi statunitensi, anche se l’incremento è stato «significativamente più contenuto» rispetto ad altri Paesi europei o agli USA.
Nonostante il contesto internazionale, non c’è pressione per un aumento dei tassi in settembre. Kalt afferma che l’inflazione svizzera, ferma allo 0,8% su base annua ad agosto, è ancora troppo bassa per giustificare un giro di vite. Hilb concorda, notando che la pressione inflazionistica rimane insufficiente e il franco troppo stabile per intervenire sui tassi di riferimento.
Link to cost-of-living Analisi pratica: cosa significano questi tassi bassi per le famiglie e le imprese svizzere? Un tasso di riferimento allo 0% riduce il costo del capitale per le imprese che intendono investire in macchinari o espansioni, mentre le famiglie trovano più accessibili i finanziamenti per l’acquisto di una casa o la ristrutturazione. Tuttavia, la remunerazione dei depositi rimane minima, spingendo molti risparmiatori verso alternative come obbligazioni corporate o fondi pensionistici.
### Confronto con i paesi vicini Negli Stati Uniti e nell’area euro, i tassi di riferimento sono rispettivamente nella forchetta 3,5‑3,75% e al 2,5%, con inflazioni più alte (2,9‑3,4%). Questo differenziale rende il franco più forte rispetto all’euro e al dollaro, sostenendo il potere d’acquisto delle importazioni ma penalizzando le esportazioni. La forza del franco è citata da Caroline Hilb come uno dei motivi per cui la BNS può mantenere i tassi bassi senza rischiare un surriscaldamento inflazionistico.
Per quanto riguarda il mercato immobiliare, l’aumento contenuto dei mutui a 10 anni (1,9%) indica che, nonostante la pressione al rialzo osservata negli USA, il costo del finanziamento abitativo in Svizzera resta relativamente basso rispetto a molti paesi europei, dove i tassi superano spesso il 2,5‑3%. Questo può sostenere la domanda di abitazioni, soprattutto nelle zone urbane di Zurigo, Ginevra e Basilea, sebbene l’offerta sia limitata da regolamenti edilizi elevati.
Infine, la bassa inflazione (0,8% in agosto) riduce l’urgenza di interventi restrittivi da parte della BNS, permettendo alla politica monetaria di sostenere la crescita senza rischiare un surriscaldamento dei prezzi. Tuttavia, gli esperti avvertono che un eventuale rialzo dei tassi negli USA potrebbe comunque trasmettersi, seppur in modo attenuato, ai mercati svizzeri, come osservato da Hilb.

What can Swiss residents actually do to take advantage of the current low interest rate situation? First of all, it is useful to compare mortgage loan offers: using the comparator of Comparis or similar instruments, you can check if your fixed or variable rate loan is still competitive compared to the average of 1.9% for 10-year mortgages.
Second, those with liquidity in bank accounts could consider shifting some of the capital to higher-yielding products, such as high-quality Swiss bonds or third-pillar pension funds, while still taking into account their own risk profile and tax implications.
